io.github.thebusybiscuit.slimefun5.utils.compatibility.packet

Class PacketWindowTitleDescriptor

  • java.lang.Object
    • io.github.thebusybiscuit.slimefun5.utils.compatibility.packet.PacketWindowTitleDescriptor

  • public final class PacketWindowTitleDescriptor
extends java.lang.Object
    Describes the clientbound open-window packet and knows how to retitle it in place, so a vanilla container's title can be corrected before the client ever renders it (rather than one tick later via InventoryView#setTitle, which still lets the wrong title flash for a frame). Resolved reflectively per server version, in the same spirit as PacketItemDescriptor: unresolvable pieces simply leave this descriptor unavailable, never a broken packet.

    • Method Detail

      • resolve

        @Nullable
public static PacketWindowTitleDescriptor resolve()
        Resolves this descriptor for the running server, or null if any of the packet class, its single component-typed title field, or a way to build a component from a plain string cannot be found - in which case window retitling stays on the (slower, one-tick-later) fallback path.
        Implementation Note:
        The title field is looked up by TYPE, never by name, and only trusted when the packet class declares exactly one such field - on server versions where the title is instead a raw (possibly JSON-encoded) String field, that would be ambiguous against the packet's other String fields (e.g. its window-type identifier), so this deliberately does not attempt a String-field fallback: getting that wrong would corrupt an unrelated field instead of just failing to retitle.

      • matches

        public boolean matches(@Nullable

      • retitle

        public boolean retitle(@Nonnull
                       java.lang.Object packet,
                       @Nonnull
                       java.lang.String text)
        Rewrites the packet's title field to text, translated into whatever chat-component representation this server version expects. Never throws - on any failure the packet is left exactly as it was (its vanilla-supplied title), which is no worse than the pre-existing flash.
